name: Mali Empire

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 1.7-1.9 million km2 for 1230-1410; Wikipedia gives 1.3 million (1350) and 1.1 million (1380) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali_Empire, low). The world_1300 polygon measures 1.75 million km2.

population.note: Seshat codes 4-5 million for 1230-1410. HYDE/OWID 1300 series for Mali, Senegal, Guinea, Mauritania and parts of Niger and Burkina Faso sum to ~3 million (low). Popular claims of 40-50 million are rejected.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Largest settlement 12,000-17,000 (Seshat); Timbuktu, Djenne, Gao and Walata trade towns.

activePersonnel.note: Standing cavalry of "around 10,000 horsemen by the reign of Mansa Musa" (via the article, drawing on al-Umari) plus the royal slave guard and household. Al-Umari (c. 1337) is a contemporary Arabic account from informants, so grade C.

trainedReserves.note: Provincial and vassal levies: al-Umari's army of ~100,000 (high; the article: "capable of 100,000 regular army", core "may have reached 90,000"). Levtzion (Ancient Ghana and Mali) relays these figures; mid halves them as a chronicler-derived number.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Somono and Bozo boat crews on the Niger, smiths, household officials.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Levy of free men of the Mande clans and vassal states.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Mailed horsemen (farari nobility) on imported North African horses, part of the ~10,000 standing cavalry.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: mail and lance on scarce large horses.

count.note: Educated guess. Lighter horsemen with javelins and bows, rest of the standing cavalry.
Educated guess. Archers (often with poisoned arrows), the core of Mande infantry.
Educated guess. Spearmen of the royal guard.
Educated guess. War canoes on the Niger crewed by Somono and Bozo boatmen.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5: Saghmandia took Gao (c. 1325); a functioning provincial system under Musa.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: clan-based levies and tributary vassals.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: expanding empire at its height.

weapons.note: Anchor 3: iron spears, swords, bows and javelins; no crossbow or trebuchet.

armor.note: Anchor 2-3: quilted cotton, leather, some imported mail for the elite.

fortification.note: Anchor 1-2: mudbrick (banco) town walls and palisades (tata).

logistics.note: Anchor 1-2: porters, donkeys, river canoes; tsetse limits horses in the south.

gdpPerCapita.note: Educated guess. No Maddison estimate for West Africa before 1950. Subsistence agriculture near the bare-bones line (~600 2011 int$), lifted by the trans-Saharan gold trade; Musa's 1324 hajj gold flooded Cairo.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Tribute and gold revenues paid for the cavalry and horse imports.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Gold mining, iron smithing, cotton weaving.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Niger floodplain rice and millet; Inner Delta surplus fed Timbuktu.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; medieval age structures were similar (high mortality, young population).

roadKm.note: Educated guess. No engineered roads; caravan tracks and the Niger.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. River ports: Kabara (Timbuktu), Djenne, Gao, Niani on the Sankarani.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. River canoes; trans-Saharan trade went by camel.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Foot and canoe armies in the Sahel; seasonal limits in the rains.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Donkeys, camels in the north, few horses (imported).

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2-1.3: Sahel distances, seasonal floods and disease the Saharan or northern invader is not adapted to.

notes: Snapshot = c. 1330, Mansa Musa (r. c. 1312-1337) after his hajj and the annexation of Gao and Timbuktu. All army numbers trace to al-Umari and Ibn Khaldun via Levtzion and the Military history of the Mali Empire article; they are informants' reports, not counts, so grade C at best. Population convention: Mali's directly governed provinces and vassal Gao and Timbuktu; Takrur and Saharan Berber tributaries excluded. The capital site (Niani) is disputed.
